messages.subject: How can I pass more backend parameters in rmr
messages.subject_clean: How can I pass more backend parameters in rmr
messages.body_plain:
Greetings.

I want to pass both number of mappers and mapred.task.timeout values as backend parameters in mapreduce API. But I am not able to do that. Both the values are required since I am running a CPU intensive simulations which will take atleast 30 mins to complete. Apart from setting the cluster value Is there anything that I can pass it via mapreduce API?

Example code that I have tried is,

mapreduce.output = from.dfs(mapreduce(paste("/tmp",filePath,sep="/"),map=map.tam,reduce=reduce.tam,input.format="text",backend.parameters = list(hadoop = list(D = "mapred.task.timeout=3600000"),hadoop = list(D = 'mapred.map.tasks=4'))))

but it doesnt seem to be working.

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#331] How can I pass more backend parameters in rmr
messages.subject_clean: [RHadoop:#331] How can I pass more backend parameters in rmr
messages.body_plain:
The syntax is slightly wrong, it should be

backend.parameters = list(hadoop = list(D = ..., D = ..., ...))

With the .. replaced by the same key value pairs you specified. But I also have to warn you that you are working at an edge case of Hadoop and it may not be the best tool for the job. Could you rephrase your computation into slightly smaller chunks even at the cost of creating some redundant input? You can have as input the iteration number for instance, even if you don't need it.

Antonio

messages.subject: Five question survey, please participate
messages.subject_clean: Five question survey, please participate
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
we need your help planning the next steps for RHadoop and we hope a survey <https://docs.google.com/spreadsheet/viewform?formkey=dFlDVEs4STF0NXZON2xEbDVMc2doUVE6MQ> will be a useful way to achieve that. It  is only five questions and they allow free text answers if you are, like me, annoyed at check lists that always miss the important points. The five questions are about use cases, data, algorithms, problems and desired features all as related to RHadoop. Please take a little time to complete the survey and forward the link to other RHadoop users. Thanks

Antonio

PS: if you missed the link: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheet/viewform?formkey=dFlDVEs4STF0NXZON2xEbDVMc2doUVE6MQ

So what I gathered from people who know Hadoop better than I do is that having a very high timeout is not a good idea and will impact fault tolerance and utilization. But I think I have found a potential workaround, based on the status string update. If one updates the status string the timeout clock is restarted. So if you have a very long computation that generates only one record of output, one solution may be to update the job status from time to time. This is not currently possible in rmr, that's why I said "potential", but we could enter a feature proposal and see if somebody takes it on.

messages.subject_clean: [RHadoop:#334] How can I pass more backend parameters in rmr
messages.body_plain:
I reopened https://github.com/RevolutionAnalytics/RHadoop/issues/14 to keep track of progress on this feature. It looks like it is enough to print to standard error

reporter:status:<message>

In R that would be achieved with

cat("reporter", "status", some.message, sep =":", file = stderr())

I suspect this should happen often enough to beat the timeout but not too often so as not to burden the system (the status update is a centralized feature and won't scale to millions of updates, I think). This way you can leave the timeout to reasonable values. You can experiment with this right now, without waiting for #14 to be resolved. While rmr doesn't allow map and reduce functions to write to stdout, writing to stderr is possible.

Antonio

On Wed, Nov 7, 2012 at 9:54 AM, Antonio Piccolboni <ant...@piccolboni.info> wrote:
> So what I gathered from people who know Hadoop better than I do is that having a very high timeout is not a good idea and will impact fault tolerance and utilization. But I think I have found a potential workaround, based on the status string update. If one updates the status string the timeout clock is restarted. So if you have a very long computation that generates only one record of output, one solution may be to update the job status from time to time. This is not currently possible in rmr, that's why I said "potential", but we could enter a feature proposal and see if somebody takes it on.
>
>
>
> On Mon, Nov 5, 2012 at 11:57 AM, Antonio Piccolboni <ant...@piccolboni.info> wrote:
> > Please provide more information. Does the job time out? Does it start but with the wrong number of mappers?  By the way I reached out to some Hadoop experts and I will try to answer your general question better (which I think can be rephrased as how to run simulations in rmr). It's an important question but the answer is not trivial.
> >
> >
> >
> > On Mon, Nov 5, 2012 at 10:28 AM, Thirumal Raman <r.thi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > I tried with backend.parameters = list(hadoop = list(D = 'mapreduce.map.tasks=3', D = 'mapred.task.timeout=360000')) and it doesnt seem to be working,
> > >
> > >
> > > On Monday, November 5, 2012 11:31:21 PM UTC+5:30, Thirumal Raman wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Thanks.
> > > >
> > > > I have a scenario where I am trying to run simulation on a multinode cluster to make use of RHadoop capabilities. I have scenario where the simulation parameters has been passed into the R code in a properties file and based upon that the mapreduce job will be invoked. Based upon the properties an intermediate file will be created with different properties in single line. I have a requirement to simulate each line in individual mapper and as of now I am able to achieve this with the help of backend properties. Is there anyother way to work with? I am not able to find anyother way....
> > > >
> > > > On Monday, November 5, 2012 10:17:21 PM UTC+5:30, Antonio Piccolboni wrote:
> > > > > The syntax is slightly wrong, it should be
> > > > >
> > > > > backend.parameters = list(hadoop = list(D = ..., D = ..., ...))
> > > > >
> > > > > With the .. replaced by the same key value pairs you specified. But I also have to warn you that you are working at an edge case of Hadoop and it may not be the best tool for the job. Could you rephrase your computation into slightly smaller chunks even at the cost of creating some redundant input? You can have as input the iteration number for instance, even if you don't need it.

messages.body_plain:
This <http://api.mongodb.org/hadoop/Hadoop+Streaming+Support.html> seems more closely related, unfortunately it requires an R parser for BSON, which doesn't exisit AFAIK.

On Thursday, November 8, 2012 11:48:40 AM UTC-8, Brock Tibert wrote:
> Is it possible to leverage RHadoop against data that is stored in MongoDB.  I see here <http://www.mongodb.org/display/DOCS/Hadoop+Quick+Start> that there is a connector, but I am not sure if these packages will allow me to embrace this format.
>
> If not, what is the best way to get my data into Hadoop so I can analyze it with R?

This is probably best asked to the mongoDB folks. rmr understand typedbytes and Json as two language agnostic formats

> Will the packages that are contained under the RHadoop umbrella allow me to both move and analyze my data?

Not move from mongoDB.

>  For context, I also have the data stored in over 700 text files, which represent hourly data collected from Twitter.  Each file stores the pure JSON responses.
>
> Simply stated, I am looking to analyze big data in R and these packages seem like a great place to start, however I am just a tad confused on how to take my data and move it between R and it's storage location.

Yes this question confuses me too. Take a look at the Tutorial or the step by step guide in the Learning Resource page on the wiki and see if there is any relation to your case. Best of all, get a hold of Ed kohwley Strata tutorial. It's all about processing twitter data. The code is linked to from the same page, the video is not yet available and will probably be for sale sometime later.

Antonio

>
> Sorry for the novice question, but any help will be greatly appreciated.

messages.subject: Need advice for using mapreduce() to mimic tapply() in producing random sets of matrices.
messages.subject_clean: Need advice for using mapreduce() to mimic tapply() in producing random sets of matrices.
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I am trying to setup an experiment where upon I fit a model to a giant block of data split up into various size subsets and find out how timings vary with subsets.  I am new to Hadoop but not R.
So to do this I started with a toy problem of trying to create, 4 2*3 matrices of random numbers, where each matrix is a value associated with keys 1, 2, 3 and 4.
Using tapply I would do this:
r.num <- rnorm(24)
keys <- rep(1:4, 6)
tapply(r.num, keys, function(x) matrix(x, nrow = 2))

So I want to mimic this using map reduce.
The first issue I found was that mapreduce() requires an input on the hdfs.  Okay, so I just send a random object to hdfs and then don't use it.
What I came up with the following.

gen.map <- function(k,v){
  r.num <- array(rnorm(24),dim=c(2,3,4))
  key <- 1:4
  kv <- NULL
  for(i in key){
    kv$key <- c(keys(kv), i)
    kv$val <- c(values(kv), list(r.num[,,i]))
  }
  return(kv)
}
a <- mapreduce(
  input = input,
  map = gen.map
)
This works, but this feels wrong.  I suspect it is inefficient.  I feel like I need a reduce step where I break up the randomly generated numbers into matrices according to their keys, just like in tapply, but I can't see the solution -- still all very new.  Can someone offer some advice?

> tapply(r.num, keys, function(x) matrix(x, nrow = 2))
>
>
> So I want to mimic this using map reduce.
> The first issue I found was that mapreduce() requires an input on the hdfs.  Okay, so I just send a random object to hdfs and then don't use it.

That will prevent you from achieving any parallelization. Yes you are running on mapreduce, but with a single map process, so what is the point?

> What I came up with the following.
>
>
> gen.map <- function(k,v){
>   r.num <- array(rnorm(24),dim=c(2,3,4))
>   key <- 1:4
>   kv <- NULL
>   for(i in key){
>     kv$key <- c(keys(kv), i)
>     kv$val <- c(values(kv), list(r.num[,,i]))
>   }
>   return(kv)
> }

Yes the for loop where you add one element at a time to the key vector is about as slow R code as you can possibly write, barring deliberate time waste. This is independent of  rmr. Also I don't recommend accessing the representation of a keyval object with $key and $val. I can't prevent you from doing so in R, but the representation can change any time. The supported interface is keys() and values(). Those are not left values, so you can't assign to them. But there is a simpler way of doing it, just call keyval(key, r.num). Unfortunately rmr doesn't support arrays yet, but you could make r.num a list of matrices, the list of the same length as the number of keys.

>
> a <- mapreduce(
>   input = input,
>   map = gen.map
> )
> This works, but this feels wrong.  I suspect it is inefficient.

It is, but not because of the missing reducer.

> I feel like I need a reduce step where I break up the randomly generated numbers into matrices according to their keys, just like in tapply,

That's not for efficiency, it's if you want the mapreduce program to be functionally equivalent to the sequential one. You are fundmentally right, reduce is equivalent to tapply.

> but I can't see the solution -- still all very new.  Can someone offer some advice?

First switch to a local backend, then't it's all local and you can debug map and reduce and see what happens. When you are ready for a big run, switch back to hadoop.  Second, you need to make your program closer to the tapply, that is it needs a reduce function  and it needs to use the tapply INDEX as keys. Next you need to create a list of matrices because we don't have support of arrays yet. In the reduce function you'll get a list of matrices as the second argument, you probably know better than I do how to go from there to an array. Maybe at some other time we need to discuss the specs to add support for arrays at the same level as there is for matrices or data frames. I hope this helps

Antonio

messages.body_plain:
I added, in the dev branch, the functions make.counter and status to update Hadoop counters and statuses. For your specific application you just need to upgrade the status at regular intervals during the computation to reset the timeout countdown. To do that, add a call like

status("still computing")

I hope this helps.

Antonio

messages.body_plain:
The only thing I can think of is to compare Rcpp version and gcc version on all three machines and see if we can spot a difference. Sometimes it looks like some neutrinos are hitting the CPU at the wrong time but more often it turns out that perfectly aligned systems are, well, not so perfectly aligned. But I'd be surprised if it compiled only one one specific version of Rcpp, which is not a bleeding edge package, I would say fairly stable at this point. But one user actually managed to find a gcc bug compiling rmr, so we need to be ready for anything.

Antonio

As you suspected there was an incompatibility of version.
Although gcc version were the same, for some reason Rcpp got updated to v0.10.0 and rmr2 was not installing properly.
Removed that version and downloaded v0.9.15 (the same that the other nodes had) and installed it through command line.

After that rmr got installed properly.

Thanks for your help and hope this issue helps out someone else.

Maybe rmr2 package need a compatibility update!

Thanks again.

On Thursday, November 15, 2012 4:31:59 PM UTC-5, Antonio Piccolboni wrote:
> The only thing I can think of is to compare Rcpp version and gcc version on all three machines and see if we can spot a difference. Sometimes it looks like some neutrinos are hitting the CPU at the wrong time but more often it turns out that perfectly aligned systems are, well, not so perfectly aligned. But I'd be surprised if it compiled only one one specific version of Rcpp, which is not a bleeding edge package, I would say fairly stable at this point. But one user actually managed to find a gcc bug compiling rmr, so we need to be ready for anything.

messages.subject: Re: Reading data from Hadoop or HDFS in R language
messages.subject_clean: Reading data from Hadoop or HDFS in R language
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
this group is about RHadoop. Rhadoop has three packages. rmr and rhdfs allow you to read from HDFS, rhbase from Hbase. We hope to make it possible for rmr to read from Hbase in the near future.

Antonio

On Tuesday, November 20, 2012 1:01:21 PM UTC+1, Prabhanjana Guttal wrote:

>
> Do we need to build any Java APIs or any standard packages available in R which reads the data directly from HDFS.
>
>
> Note: Both R and Hadoop are running on Ubuntu OS.
>
> regards,
> Prabhanjana

messages.subject: Debugging with logs
messages.subject_clean: Debugging with logs
messages.body_plain:
Greetings.

I am able to RHadoop jobs with thousands of mappers. There is an occasional problem occurring in the system that the values between the different keys are mixed up and written in the mappers. When I try to debug with mappers logs and reducers logs, it became cumbersome since it has thousands of files spread across multiple nodes in the cluster. Is there any mechanism n RHadoop to do a central logging of the logs (i.e.) using a scribe server.

(E.g.) http://blog.cloudera.com/blog/2008/11/configuring-and-using-scribe-for-hadoop-log-collection/

messages.subject_clean: Toy example from airplane data tutorial throwing errors.
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to implement the example code for the Airline dataset given in Jeffrey Breen's tutorial found here <http://www.slideshare.net/jeffreybreen/big-data-stepbystep-using-r-hadoop-with-rhadoops-rmr-package#btnNext>.  I haven't been successful.

In my input directory I have a csv file with lines that look like this
 2004,3,25,4,1445,1437,1820,1812,AA,399,N275AA,215,215,197,8,8,BOS,MIA,1258,6,12,0,,0,0,0,0,0,0
I am using only one input file, it is a csv containing only a subset of the true dataset -- only about 5,000 lines.

I went though the code within the formatting, map, and reduce functions with example inputs and it all works fine.

When I run the code I get the error;
Error in mr(map = map, reduce = reduce, combine = combine, in.folder = if (is.list(input)) { :
  hadoop streaming failed with error code 5
In addition: Warning message:
In mapreduce(input = input, output = output, input.format = asa.csvtextinputformat,  :
  backend.parameters is deprecated.

Can someone tell me what I am missing? Thanks.  Code below.

library(rmr2)
hdfs.input.path <- "/usr/cloudera/airline/data/in"

asa.csvtextinputformat <- make.input.format(format = function(line){
  values <- unlist(strsplit(line, "\\,"))
  names(values) <- c("Year", "Month", "DayofMonth", "DayofWeek", "DepTime",
    "CRSDepTime", "ArrTime", "CRSArrTime", "UniqueCarrier",
    "FlightNum", "TailNum", "ActualElapsedTime", "CRSElapsedTime",
    "AirTime", "ArrDelay", "DepDelay", "Origin", "Dest", "Distance",
    "TaxiIn", "TaxiOut", "Cancelled", "CancellationCode", "Diverted",
    "CarrierDelay", "WeatherDelay", "NASDelay",
    "SecurityDelay", "LateAircraftDelay")
  return(keyval(NULL, values))
})

mapper.year.market.enroute_time <- function(key, val){
  #Skip header lines, cancellations, and diversions:
  if(!identical(as.character(val['Year']),'Year')
     &identical(as.numeric(val['Cancelled']),0)
     &identical(as.numeric(val['Diverted']),0)){

    #We don't care about direction of travel, so construct 'market'
    #with airports ordered alphabetically (e.g, LAX to JFK becomes 'JFK-LAX'
    if(val['Origin'] < val['Dest']){
      market <- paste(val['Origin'], val['Dest'], sep='-')
      } else market <- paste(val['Dest'], val['Origin'], sep='-')
    # key consists of year,market
    output.key=c(val['Year'],market)

    #output gate-to-gate elapsed times(CRSandactual) + time in airoutput.
    output.val=c(val['CRSElapsedTime'],val['ActualElapsedTime'],val['AirTime'])

    return(keyval(output.key,output.val))
  }
}

reducer.year.market.enroute_time = function(key, val.list){
  if(require(plyr)) val.df = ldply(val.list, as.numeric) else{
    #this is as close as my deficient * apply skills can come w/o
    plyrval.list = lapply(val.list, as.numeric)
    val.df = data.frame(do.call(rbind, val.list))
  }
  colnames(val.df) = c('actual','crs','air')
  output.key = key
  output.val = c(nrow(val.df), mean(val.df$actual,na.rm=T), mean(val.df$crs, na.rm = T), mean(val.df$air,na.rm = T))
  return(keyval(output.key, output.val))
}

mr.year.market.enroute_time = function(input,output){
  mapreduce(input = input,
            output = output,
            input.format = asa.csvtextinputformat,
            map = mapper.year.market.enroute_time,
            reduce = reducer.year.market.enroute_time,
            backend.parameters = list(hadoop= list(D="mapred.reduce.tasks=10")),
            verbose=T)
}
hdfs.output.root <- "/usr/cloudera/airline/data/out"
hdfs.output.path = file.path(hdfs.output.root,'enroute-time')
results = mr.year.market.enroute_time(hdfs.input.path, hdfs.output.path)

messages.subject: Re: Install rmr2 in a local directory
messages.subject_clean: Install rmr2 in a local directory
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the excellent report and detailed analysis. I think you are right as far as what the problem is, but I don't have a solution. It will take some experiments and I suspect even a patch. I am on trip right now and with on and off internet access it's hard for me to look into this but I will give it a try late next week. If you are so advanced as to be willing to write a patch yourself, you can add a libpaths assignment just before line 148 ("invisible...") and see if that fixes it. It's a hack but it would tell me what is needed in a more acceptable solution. The other thing to worry about is if that path is available on every node in the cluster. It wouldn't be  the most common case of a cluster node with user directories mounted. Also make sure not to rely on ~ expansion, as the user as which the jobs are run is a special hadoop user, not your login user.

Antonio

Sure.
I just wonder if we can take control of the number of reducers. (If the keys are too many to fit in size of the main memory?)

First the data set is from this page http://fimi.ua.ac.be/data/
The last data set on that page -- webdocs.dat.gz (1.4Gb when unzipped)

The code is

#  1692082 //Total redords (1.4Gb)

library(rmr2)
library(arules)

##  Local apriori finding frequent itemsets with !support=0.5!
        readRows <- function(file, sep="\n", split=" ", ...){
        tt <- strsplit(
                        scan(file, what="list", sep=sep, ...),
                        split=split)
                out <- lapply(tt, function(i) as.numeric(i))
                out
}

        webdoc <- readRows('/home/hduser/data/webdoc-10000.dat')
        tr_webdoc <- as(webdoc, "transactions")
        fItemL <- apriori(tr_webdoc, parameter=new("APparameter", support=0.5,target="frequent itemsets", maxlen=5))

##  paralell-apriori finding frequent itemsets with !support=0.3!
##  Reason: Because we are finding "local" frequent itemset's support count in the mapper, then in the reducer we accumulate the support count for each local-frequent itemset. (An itemset with global support 0.5 will not have local support of 0.5 on every datanode, so we will find relative lower local-support 0.3 itemset's support count in the mapper. Then after the mapreduce we can get global-frequent itemset with a higher support by elimanating itemsets below the higher support 0.5, see below.)

        papriori =
          function(
                input,
                output = NULL,
                pattern = " ",
                support=0.3,
                maxlen=5 #This is important!
                ){

                        ## papriori-map
                        pa.map =
                          function(., lines) {
                                if((LL=length(lines))>5000){
                                fItems <- apriori(as(lapply(strsplit(
                                                                               x = lines,
                                                                               split = pattern), unique),
                                                                        "transactions"),
                                                                parameter=new("APparameter",
                                                                               support=support,
                                                                               target="frequent itemsets",
                                                                               maxlen=maxlen))

                                recNum <- fItems@info$ntransactions[1]

                                keyval(as(items(fItems), "list"),
                                        fItems@quality$support*recNum)}
                                else
                                keyval(list("-1"),LL) #Number of records skiped.
                        }

                        ## papiori-reduce
                        pa.reduce =
                          function(word, counts ) {
                                keyval(word, sum(counts))}

                        ## papiori-mapreduce
                        mapreduce(
                          input = input ,
                          output = output,
                          input.format = "text",
                          map = pa.map,
                          reduce = pa.reduce,
                          combine = T)
        }

        rmr.options(backend = "hadoop")
        rmr.options(keyval.length=10000)

        out.hadoop = from.dfs(papriori("/user/hduser/webdoc", pattern = " +"))

        items <- out.hadoop$key
        distinSkip <- function(x) {
        indicator=FALSE
        if(length(unlist(x))>1)
        indicator=FALSE
        else if(unlist(x)==-1)
        indicator=TRUE
        else
        indicator=FALSE
        }

        skipedNumRec <- out.hadoop$val[unlist(lapply(items, distinSkip))]
        skipedNumRec

        totalNumRec<-1692082 #Total number of records
        supportH<-out.hadoop$val/(totalNumRec-skipedNumRec)
        biggerSup<-supportH>0.5
        webKey <- out.hadoop$key[biggerSup]
        webVal <- supportH[biggerSup]
        fItemH<-new("itemsets")
        fItemH@items<-as(webKey,"transactions")
        fItemH@quality<-data.frame(support=webVal)
        inspect(fItemH)

        inspect(fItemL)

Chao

messages.body_plain:
apriori algorithm is used to find frequent itemsets and association rules efficiently by pruning infrequent candidates.
The problem here we are trying to address is to find frequent itemsets in a large amount of transaction data. RHadoop give us the ability to find locally frequent itemsets in the mapper, then reducer aggregates the support count for each locally frequent itemset in order to get the global support count for global frequent itemsets.
It's great that we can control how many records are fed to the mapper each time. The global frequent itemsets may not be(or should not be) locally frequent on every fraction of the data, so increasing the size of the local data set will narrow down the probability of such cases.
I use the webdoc dataset to mimic transaction data. Each line of the webdoc dataset contains the words appeared in a webpage. Applying apriori on the dataset will give us which combination of words appeared most frequently. It gives us ability to find frequent itemsets from big transaction data parallelly and efficiently. 14 minutes to mining 1.4Gb 1690000 records of data.

https://github.com/RevolutionAnalytics/RHadoop/wiki/Finding-Frequent-Itemsets

I did minimal editing and reindented the code in RStudio. Credits at the bottom. The only thing I would like to add is a line on the hardware that got you those timing results.

On Tue, Nov 27, 2012 at 7:02 AM, Antonio Piccolboni <ant...@piccolboni.info> wrote:
> Wonderful, thanks!
>
>
> On Tue, Nov 27, 2012 at 12:45 AM, cyang05 <superm...@163.com> wrote:
> > apriori algorithm is used to find frequent itemsets and association rules efficiently by pruning infrequent candidates.
> > The problem here we are trying to address is to find frequent itemsets in a large amount of transaction data. RHadoop give us the ability to find locally frequent itemsets in the mapper, then reducer aggregates the support count for each locally frequent itemset in order to get the global support count for global frequent itemsets.
> > It's great that we can control how many records are fed to the mapper each time. The global frequent itemsets may not be(or should not be) locally frequent on every fraction of the data, so increasing the size of the local data set will narrow down the probability of such cases.
> > I use the webdoc dataset to mimic transaction data. Each line of the webdoc dataset contains the words appeared in a webpage. Applying apriori on the dataset will give us which combination of words appeared most frequently. It gives us ability to find frequent itemsets from big transaction data parallelly and efficiently. 14 minutes to mining 1.4Gb 1690000 records of data.
> >
> > On Monday, November 26, 2012 12:20:10 AM UTC-6, Antonio Piccolboni wrote:
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > On Sun, Nov 25, 2012 at 10:42 PM, cyang05 <superm...@163.com> wrote:
> > > > Sure.
> > > > I just wonder if we can take control of the number of reducers. (If the keys are too many to fit in size of the main memory?)
> > >
> > > The reducers do not load all the keys into memory, they use a streaming approach.
> > > Thanks for sharing your code, could you add a paragraph describing the problem and the solution? Thanks
> > >
> > > Antonio
> > >
> > > >
> > > > First the data set is from this page http://fimi.ua.ac.be/data/
> > > > The last data set on that page -- webdocs.dat.gz (1.4Gb when unzipped)
> > > >
> > > > The code is
> > > >
> > > > #  1692082 //Total redords (1.4Gb)
> > > >
> > > > library(rmr2)
> > > > library(arules)
> > > >
> > > > ##  Local apriori finding frequent itemsets with !support=0.5!
> > > >         readRows <- function(file, sep="\n", split=" ", ...){
> > > >         tt <- strsplit(
> > > >                         scan(file, what="list", sep=sep, ...),
> > > >                         split=split)
> > > >                 out <- lapply(tt, function(i) as.numeric(i))
> > > >                 out
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > >         webdoc <- readRows('/home/hduser/data/webdoc-10000.dat')
> > > >         tr_webdoc <- as(webdoc, "transactions")
> > > >         fItemL <- apriori(tr_webdoc, parameter=new("APparameter", support=0.5,target="frequent itemsets", maxlen=5))
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > ##  paralell-apriori finding frequent itemsets with !support=0.3!
> > > > ##  Reason: Because we are finding "local" frequent itemset's support count in the mapper, then in the reducer we accumulate the support count for each local-frequent itemset. (An itemset with global support 0.5 will not have local support of 0.5 on every datanode, so we will find relative lower local-support 0.3 itemset's support count in the mapper. Then after the mapreduce we can get global-frequent itemset with a higher support by elimanating itemsets below the higher support 0.5, see below.)
> > > >
> > > >         papriori =
> > > >           function(
> > > >                 input,
> > > >                 output = NULL,
> > > >                 pattern = " ",
> > > >                 support=0.3,
> > > >                 maxlen=5 #This is important!
> > > >                 ){
> > > >
> > > >                         ## papriori-map
> > > >                         pa.map =
> > > >                           function(., lines) {
> > > >                                 if((LL=length(lines))>5000){
> > > >                                 fItems <- apriori(as(lapply(strsplit(
> > > >                                                                                x = lines,
> > > >                                                                                split = pattern), unique),
> > > >                                                                         "transactions"),
> > > >                                                                 parameter=new("APparameter",
> > > >                                                                                support=support,
> > > >                                                                                target="frequent itemsets",
> > > >                                                                                maxlen=maxlen))
> > > >
> > > >                                 recNum <- fItems@info$ntransactions[1]
> > > >
> > > >                                 keyval(as(items(fItems), "list"),
> > > >                                         fItems@quality$support*recNum)}
> > > >                                 else
> > > >                                 keyval(list("-1"),LL) #Number of records skiped.
> > > >                         }
> > > >
> > > >                         ## papiori-reduce
> > > >                         pa.reduce =
> > > >                           function(word, counts ) {
> > > >                                 keyval(word, sum(counts))}
> > > >
> > > >                         ## papiori-mapreduce
> > > >                         mapreduce(
> > > >                           input = input ,
> > > >                           output = output,
> > > >                           input.format = "text",
> > > >                           map = pa.map,
> > > >                           reduce = pa.reduce,
> > > >                           combine = T)
> > > >         }
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >         rmr.options(backend = "hadoop")
> > > >         rmr.options(keyval.length=10000)
> > > >
> > > >         out.hadoop = from.dfs(papriori("/user/hduser/webdoc", pattern = " +"))
> > > >
> > > >         items <- out.hadoop$key
> > > >         distinSkip <- function(x) {
> > > >         indicator=FALSE
> > > >         if(length(unlist(x))>1)
> > > >         indicator=FALSE
> > > >         else if(unlist(x)==-1)
> > > >         indicator=TRUE
> > > >         else
> > > >         indicator=FALSE
> > > >         }
> > > >
> > > >         skipedNumRec <- out.hadoop$val[unlist(lapply(items, distinSkip))]
> > > >         skipedNumRec
> > > >
> > > >         totalNumRec<-1692082 #Total number of records
> > > >         supportH<-out.hadoop$val/(totalNumRec-skipedNumRec)
> > > >         biggerSup<-supportH>0.5
> > > >         webKey <- out.hadoop$key[biggerSup]
> > > >         webVal <- supportH[biggerSup]
> > > >         fItemH<-new("itemsets")
> > > >         fItemH@items<-as(webKey,"transactions")
> > > >         fItemH@quality<-data.frame(support=webVal)
> > > >         inspect(fItemH)
> > > >
> > > >         inspect(fItemL)
> > > >
> > > > Chao
> > > >
> > > > On Sunday, November 25, 2012 3:22:58 PM UTC-6, Antonio Piccolboni wrote:

> > > > >

> > > > > > The whole data set has 1692082 transaction records.

> > > > > >
> > > > > > The succeeded run took 12 min 36 sec. (10 VMs, 1 master node and 9 slave nodes.)
> > > > > > The code is pretty simple. (Some preprocessing the data, remove duplicates)
> > > > > > It's the apriori algorithm from package(arules), looking for frequent itemsets.

> > > > > > 9  {49,
> > > > > >     8}   0.6308027
> > > > > > 10 {124} 0.5244245
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks for the report, it's rewarding for people trying to solve user issues to know that they were actually solved.
> > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > By the way, how can I control the number of reducers to run?
> > > > >
> > > > > Can I ask you first why you need to do that? There usually is a better way to do what you need to do than tampering with the number of reducers.
> > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I would like you to put my code to the tutorial section of RHadoop if possible. It's association rule mining in the data mining world.
> > > > >
> > > > > Awesome, how about you publish it here as a reply first and then  I move it to the wiki? Maybe not the Tutorial, but I will create a use cases page or some such.
> > > > >
> > > > > Antonio
> > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thanks.

> > > > > >

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#421] Memory limitations of RHadoop?
messages.subject_clean: [RHadoop:#421] Memory limitations of RHadoop?
messages.body_plain:
RHadoop is a collection of three packages. rhdfs and rhbase run within a single R instance and load data in memory directly, I would say they are mostly subject to memory limitations (I say mostly because you can probably code your way around it by reading subsets of the data). rmr instead adopts the mapreduce model, therefore loads into memory only a subset of the data by default. You can still run into memory problems with very large records or if you have a small set of keys in the reduce phase but at least you have a powerful tool to address the problem. It's  no magic bullet, algorithms still need to be designed by humans using their intellect.

Antonio

On Fri, Nov 30, 2012 at 10:56 AM, MarkP <mark.p...@nokia.com> wrote:
> On Friday, November 30, 2012 11:01:51 AM UTC-6, Antonio Piccolboni wrote:
> > RHadoop is a collection of three packages. rhdfs and rhbase run within a single R instance and load data in memory directly, I would say they are mostly subject to memory limitations (I say mostly because you can probably code your way around it by reading subsets of the data). rmr instead adopts the mapreduce model, therefore loads into memory only a subset of the data by default.
>
> Is this because rmr splits the data across multiple map tasks?

Yes and no. Hadoop is in charge of the task split and rmr leverages hadoop for that. In addition, each task reads a bunch of records, calls the map function and writes the return value out (hadoop takes it from there). So we have a split by task and a streaming kind of approach to each task.

> Does it eventually work its way through the entire input data?

Of course. I am not sure what happens if you exit the process from the mapper, there is nothing to prevent you from doing that but you may get a broken pipe error at the Hadoop level. Actually I've just run a few experiments and it seems to work. You actually gave me an idea to improve rmr.sample. Take this with a grain of salt but it appears you can quit from the mapper (let's say after you read enough data for your goals or you found a record of interest).

>
> > You can still run into memory problems with very large records or if you have a small set of keys in the reduce phase
>
> Is the number of keys relevant because it determines the number of reduce tasks?

No it determines the number of reduce calls. Each reduce task makes multiple reduce calls, one per key. Very little data is preserved between calls (unless you reducer explicitly stores it). The number of reduce processes  depends on the Hadoop configuration.

Antonio
